text:
**The Keeper of Hollow Lane**

The old abandoned house at the end of the street held a secret that no one had ever discovered.

Everyone on Hollow Lane had a theory, of course. Mrs. Pemberton swore it was a murder. The Delgado twins insisted it was haunted by a woman in gray who appeared at the attic window on foggy nights. Old Mr. Finch, who had lived across from it for fifty-one years, said nothing at all. He only drew his curtains a little tighter when the sun went down.

Eleven-year-old Nora Vance didn't believe in ghosts. She believed in evidence. So on the first Saturday of October, with a flashlight, a notebook, and a peanut butter sandwich in her backpack, she squeezed through the gap in the iron fence and walked up the cracked path to the front door.

It opened before she touched it.

Nora stood very still. The hinges hadn't creaked. The door had simply swung inward, smooth as breath, as though someone had been waiting.

"Hello?" she called.

Dust hung in the slanted afternoon light. The foyer was grander than she'd imagined: a curving staircase, a chandelier draped in cobwebs like lace, wallpaper patterned with faded birds. And clocks. Dozens of them. Grandfather clocks lined the hallway, cuckoo clocks crowded the walls, and pocket watches dangled from nails like strange fruit.

Every one of them had stopped at 4:17.

Nora wrote it down. *All clocks: 4:17. Why?*

She checked her own watch. 4:16.

The minute hand ticked forward.

At once the house *exhaled*. Every clock shuddered to life, a hundred pendulums swinging, a hundred second hands sweeping, a rising chorus of ticking that filled her chest like a heartbeat. The dust in the air froze mid-drift, then began, impossibly, to rise *upward*, back toward the ceiling, back into the corners it had fallen from.

The cobwebs unraveled. The wallpaper birds deepened from gray to blue and gold. Somewhere upstairs, a piano began to play.

"Don't be frightened," said a voice.

A woman stood at the top of the staircase. She wore a gray dress with a high collar, and her hair was pinned the way women wore it in old photographs. She was not transparent, not glowing, not anything like the ghosts in the Delgado twins' stories. She looked tired, and kind, and very, very relieved.

"You're the woman in the window," Nora whispered.

"I suppose I am." The woman descended slowly. "My name is Eleanor Finch. And you, I think, are the first person in fifty-one years to walk through that door at exactly the right minute."

*Finch.* Nora's pencil stopped.

"This house keeps time for the whole street," Eleanor said, touching the face of a grandfather clock with great tenderness. "That was my family's charge, generations of us. As long as the clocks run, Hollow Lane stays… held. Safe. Gardens bloom, children grow up healthy, storms pass around it. But the clocks must be wound by a Keeper, and a Keeper cannot leave."

"What happened at 4:17?"

Eleanor's face softened with an old grief. "I was twenty-two. I fell in love with a young man from across the street. He asked me to leave with him, to see the world. I said yes." She smiled sadly. "I stepped outside the door at 4:17 and the clocks stopped. And I've been caught in between ever since: not here, not gone. Only the house remembering me."

"And the young man?"

"He waited. I think he's waiting still."

Nora thought of Mr. Finch, drawing his curtains every night. Never moving away. Never marrying. Fifty-one years of watching the attic window.

"He took your name," she said slowly. "Didn't he? Or you took his. You were going to get married."

Eleanor's eyes shone.

The clocks were growing louder. Nora glanced at her watch: 4:17 and forty seconds.

"What happens when the minute ends?" she asked.

"The house falls asleep again. Perhaps for another fifty years. Perhaps forever." Eleanor knelt so they were eye to eye. "Unless someone chooses to keep the time in my place. Just long enough for me to walk out that door properly."

Nora understood then. This was the secret. Not a murder, not a haunting. A trade.

Forty-five seconds. Fifty.

She looked at the clocks, all those patient faces. She thought of her street: the maple trees that never seemed to lose limbs in storms, the way Hollow Lane had never once flooded when the rest of town did. She thought of an old man behind his curtains.

"How long?" Nora asked. "How long would I have to stay?"

Eleanor blinked, as though no one had ever thought to ask. "Only until someone comes to wind them with you. A Keeper doesn't have to be alone. I only was because I was afraid to ask."

Fifty-five seconds.

Nora took off her backpack and set it on the floor. She pulled out her notebook and, on a fresh page, wrote in her neatest handwriting:

*Help wanted: Keeper of Clocks. Must be good with time. Must not be afraid of the dark. Inquire within.*

She tore it out and handed it to Eleanor.

"Pin it to the fence on your way out," Nora said. "And tell Mr. Finch to come over. I think he's very good at waiting."

The minute hand clicked to 4:18.

The front door opened onto golden October light. Eleanor Finch stepped through it, and this time the clocks did not stop.

Across the street, a curtain was flung open. An old man stood frozen in his window. Then he was out his front door, faster than he had moved in decades, crossing Hollow Lane in his slippers, and the woman in gray was running too, and they met in the middle of the road where the maple leaves were falling.

Inside the house, Nora Vance picked up a brass winding key, found the nearest grandfather clock, and got to work.

She was going to need a bigger notebook.

---

*The house at the end of Hollow Lane isn't abandoned anymore. If you walk past at dusk, you'll see lamplight in the windows and hear a hundred clocks ticking in perfect time. And on the iron fence, weathered but still legible, hangs a small handwritten sign.*

*They're still hiring.*
